faqs.answer: Size and foam. A cappuccino is a 5 to 6 oz drink in equal thirds with a thick foam cap. A latte is an 8 to 12 oz drink at 1:5 espresso to milk with only a thin layer of foam.

faqs.answer: Usually the milk was not aerated enough, or it was steamed too hot. Aerate the milk early in the steam, keep it at 60 to 65 C, and use whole milk for the most stable foam.

formula.text: Milk = espresso × 2. Espresso = milk ÷ 2. The milk splits into one part liquid and one part foam.

howToSteps.name: Pull a double shot
howToSteps.text: Dose 18 g of fine coffee and pull 36 g of espresso in 25 to 30 seconds, straight into a 6 oz cup.

howToSteps.name: Steam the milk
howToSteps.text: Steam 72 g of cold whole milk to 60 to 65 C, aerating it well so half of it becomes thick foam, about a centimetre and a half deep.

howToSteps.name: Pour the milk, then the foam
howToSteps.text: Pour the liquid milk into the espresso first, then spoon the foam on top. The cup should be a third espresso, a third milk, a third foam.

howToSteps.name: Serve straight away
howToSteps.text: Dust with cocoa if you like, and serve at once. The foam starts to break down within a couple of minutes.

title: Espresso to Milk Ratio for Cappuccino
tutorial: A cappuccino is the tidiest drink on the menu: equal thirds of espresso, steamed milk, and foam. One part espresso, one part milk, one part foam, in a 5 to 6 oz cup. That is a 1:2 espresso to milk ratio, because the milk you steam splits into the liquid third and the foam third.

A double shot of 36 g takes 72 g of milk. Half of that milk stays liquid and half becomes foam, so the finished drink is a third espresso, a third milk, and a third foam. The foam is the difference between a cappuccino and a flat white, which uses the same milk but almost no foam.

Modern cafes often brew a milkier cappuccino, closer to 1:4 espresso to milk, in a bigger cup. That is a real variation, not a mistake, but it is not the classic drink. The classic is small, strong, and foam-heavy, and it is the one this calculator uses. The range is worth knowing if a cafe cappuccino tastes different from yours.

Steam the milk to 60 to 65 C, 140 to 150 F, and aerate it more than you would for a latte. The foam should be thick and airy, about a centimetre and a half deep, and it should sit on top of the drink instead of mixing in. Whole milk gives the most stable foam.

Pour the milk first, then spoon the foam on top. That is the old-fashioned way, and it is still the easiest way to get the thirds right at home. The drink should be finished and served within a minute or two, before the foam starts to break down.
